strategy_title: Autotune Larger XBLOCK Caused Register Spill Regression
strategy_description: Adding @triton.autotune with larger XBLOCK values (512–2048) caused the compiler to allocate significantly more registers per thread (18→32), reducing Block Limit Registers from 21 to 16 and cutting theoretical warp slots. Although achieved occupancy rose (61.6%→87.0%) and compute throughput increased (61.9%→80.1%), the total executed instruction count nearly doubled (9.3M→17.0M) and kernel duration increased by 41% (19.3→27.2 µs). The FMA fix (int32/float→float reciprocal) did not compensate for the instruction explosion caused by the larger tile size interacting with register pressure and loop unrolling.
slow_pseudocode:
# XBLOCK=128, 18 registers/thread, grid=27000
@triton.jit
def kernel(...):
    tmp6 = tl.sqrt_rn(tmp5)
    tmp7 = tl.full([1], 1, tl.int32)
    tmp8 = (tmp7 / tmp6)  # int32 reciprocal
    tmp9 = tl.full([1], 1.0, tl.float32)
    tmp10 = tmp8 * tmp9   # no-op multiply
    tmp11 = tmp2 * tmp10
grid = (cdiv(xnumel, 128),)
kernel[grid](..., XBLOCK=128)
applicable_when: Never apply this specific combination when the kernel already has low register count (≤20 registers/thread) and the autotune configs include very large XBLOCK values that may trigger aggressive loop unrolling and register pressure increase.
do_not_apply_when: Do not apply autotune with large XBLOCK (≥512) on kernels where the baseline register count is already near the block-limit-register boundary, or where the instruction count is expected to scale super-linearly with XBLOCK due to unrolling. Also avoid when the grid is already large (>10K CTAs) and occupancy gap is primarily due to warp scheduling rather than insufficient warps.
framework_notes: In Triton, @triton.autotune with large XBLOCK values can cause the compiler to unroll inner loops more aggressively, increasing register pressure beyond what the baseline kernel uses. The grid lambda must match the autotuned XBLOCK, but if the static grid (cdiv(xnumel, 128)) is passed instead of the dynamic lambda, the kernel runs with the wrong grid size regardless of the autotuned XBLOCK—this is a common implementation flaw. Verify the grid is a lambda when using autotune.

strategy_title: Autotune Larger XBLOCK Causes Register Pressure Regression
strategy_description: Adding @triton.autotune with larger XBLOCK configs (512–2048) caused registers per thread to jump from 18 to 32, nearly doubling total executed instructions (9.3M → 17.0M) and increasing kernel duration from 19.3 µs to 27.14 µs despite improving achieved occupancy (61.6% → 86.7%). The instruction count explosion indicates the compiler unrolled more aggressively or generated additional spill/fill code at larger tile sizes, overwhelming any benefit from wider memory transactions. When the baseline kernel already has low register usage and the bottleneck is L1TEX stalls, increasing XBLOCK without controlling register pressure via `num_stages` or `maxnreg` can cause more harm than good.

    xindex = xoffset + tl.arange(0, XBLOCK)[:]
    # pointwise BN + hardtanh body
    tl.store(in_out_ptr0 + x2, result, xmask)

grid = (triton.cdiv(xnumel, 128),)
kernel[grid](arg_0, ..., xnumel, XBLOCK=128)
applicable_when: Never apply this pattern as described. The autotune approach with large XBLOCK configs is harmful when the baseline kernel has low register count (≤20 registers/thread) and the grid is already static (not a lambda). The static grid does not adapt to the autotuned XBLOCK, so the kernel may run with a mismatched grid.
do_not_apply_when: Do not increase XBLOCK via autotune when: (1) baseline registers per thread are already low (≤20) and larger tiles cause register count to nearly double; (2) the grid is not updated to a lambda that reads meta['XBLOCK'], causing a mismatch between grid size and tile size; (3) the instruction count increase from unrolling outweighs memory transaction savings. Also avoid when the kernel is already compute-bound (Compute SM Throughput > 60%) rather than purely memory-latency-bound.
framework_notes: In Triton, when using @triton.autotune, the grid MUST be a lambda `lambda meta: (triton.cdiv(xnumel, meta['XBLOCK']),)` — not a static tuple — otherwise the grid size does not adapt to the chosen XBLOCK config. The diff shows the grid was left as a static tuple `(triton.cdiv(xnumel, 128),)`, which is an implementation flaw compounding the register pressure issue.

strategy_title: Doubling num_warps at Fixed XBLOCK Caused Instruction Explosion
strategy_description: Increasing num_warps from 4 to 8 at XBLOCK=128 (and allowing XBLOCK=256 configs) caused the autotune to select XBLOCK=256 with 256 threads/block, which doubled executed instructions (9.3M → 18.7M) and increased kernel duration by 64% (19.26 µs → 31.62 µs). Although eligible warps per scheduler improved (1.84 → 3.75) and achieved occupancy rose (61.0% → 81.2%), the instruction count explosion from the larger tile size overwhelmed any latency-hiding benefit. Even though registers per thread only rose modestly (18 → 21), the doubling of total threads (3.46M → 6.91M) and waves per SM (12.78 → 25.57) indicates the autotune selected the wider XBLOCK=256 config, not the intended XBLOCK=128/num_warps=8 config, causing the regression.
slow_pseudocode:
# AFTER (regressed) — autotune selected XBLOCK=256, block_size=256
@triton.autotune(configs=[
    Config({'XBLOCK': 128}, num_warps=8,  num_stages=1),
    Config({'XBLOCK': 128}, num_warps=4,  num_stages=1),
    Config({'XBLOCK': 128}, num_warps=16, num_stages=1),
    Config({'XBLOCK': 256}, num_warps=8,  num_stages=1),  # <-- selected
    Config({'XBLOCK': 256}, num_warps=16, num_stages=1),
], key=['xnumel'])
@triton.jit
def kernel(..., XBLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    # pointwise BN + hardtanh body
    ...
grid = lambda meta: (cdiv(xnumel, meta['XBLOCK']),)
kernel[grid](...)  # autotune selected XBLOCK=256, 18.7M instructions
fast_pseudocode:
# BEFORE (baseline) — static XBLOCK=128, block_size=128
@triton.jit
def kernel(..., XBLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    # pointwise BN + hardtanh body
    ...
grid = (cdiv(xnumel, 128),)
kernel[grid](..., XBLOCK=128)  # 9.3M instructions, 19.26 µs
applicable_when: Never apply this pattern on short-duration pointwise kernels (<25 µs) where the autotune config space includes XBLOCK values larger than the baseline, even if the intent is only to increase num_warps at the same XBLOCK. The autotune will select the wider tile if it appears faster during warmup, causing instruction count to scale with XBLOCK.
do_not_apply_when: Do not add larger XBLOCK configs to the autotune search space when: (1) the baseline kernel is already short-duration (<25 µs) and compute-bound (Compute SM Throughput >60%); (2) the instruction count is expected to scale linearly or super-linearly with XBLOCK due to pointwise unrolling; (3) the goal is only to increase num_warps without changing tile size — in that case, restrict autotune configs strictly to the baseline XBLOCK value only. Also avoid when waves per SM are already >10, as additional occupancy gains from more warps per block yield diminishing returns.
framework_notes: In Triton, when using @triton.autotune to increase num_warps, including any XBLOCK value larger than the baseline in the config list risks the autotuner selecting the wider tile, which doubles thread count and instruction count for pointwise kernels. To safely increase num_warps only, restrict all configs to a single XBLOCK value equal to the baseline (e.g., only XBLOCK=128 configs with varying num_warps). The grid lambda correctly adapts to the autotuned XBLOCK, but this also means a wider XBLOCK will run with fewer grid blocks and more work per block — the opposite of the intended effect when targeting latency hiding.
